Love, screenprint

Robert Indiana’s LOVE in a 1967 screenprint: four red slab-serif letters stacked two over two, with a tilted O, on flat blue and green.

Source
V&A: Love, CIRC.579-1968
Creator
Robert Indiana
Made
1967
Style
Pop art (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Bold, emblematic, commercial
Evidence
Downloaded and inspected the V&A image of its copy, CIRC.579-1968 (1200 × 1456 px), in a scratchpad. No image is stored.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

The V&A records a colour screenprint on paper, 65 × 50 cm, printed by Editions Domberger in 1967. It calls the image one of the iconic images of American Pop Art and notes that it was used for a US postage stamp. V&A.

A sister print in the V&A (CIRC.576-1968) belongs to a set of four called “Love Wall”, made for a portfolio published in Germany for the exhibition Formen der Farbe. V&A.

The 1973 US stamp is recorded as LOVE stamp.

Observed

  • The letters L, O, V, and E are stacked in a square, LO above VE, and fill the image to its edges.
  • The letters are flat red slab-serif capitals. The O is tilted to the right, and its counter is a green oblong.
  • The spaces between the letters are flat blue in the top half and flat green in the bottom half.
  • Red and green, and red and blue, meet at hard edges with no outline between them.
  • A wide unprinted white margin fills the bottom of the sheet.

Why it belongs

Indiana’s contribution to the idiom is the word as image: sign-painter lettering, enlarged until the letters become the whole composition.

The red against blue and green vibrates at the edges, so the image stays loud without any black line.

Borrow

Stack a short word in heavy slab-serif capitals into a square and let it fill the panel.

Tilt one letter to give a static block of type a single point of movement.
